mark_split.label: Divide, then set up the form

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.67 — SAQ chapter 11 Partial Fractions, answer 101 (the book's 'TYPE 3 [deg(Nr) ≥ deg(Dr)]', the first improper fraction). Printed appearances: AP 19. ⚠ THE 1+1+1+1 SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — this chapter prints no [N Marks] tags against any answer, only tick boxes. The split is the four moves of the method (set up the form · clear the denominators · find the constants · write the result), one mark each, and the SAME split and the SAME step ids (s1_form, s2_identity, s3_constants, s4_result) are used on all fifteen cards of this unit, deliberately: they are one method over different fractions. For the improper fractions the division lives inside s1_form, and for the (x − 3)³ question the substitution x − 3 = y takes the place of the form. The book's SAQ chapter header carries ★★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-2A Section B runs Q11–Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q15 is the Partial Fractions slot (the chapter has no Section A or Section C slot). Not asked at Q15 in any of the five model papers. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper — recorded, not hidden. A back-test against the book's own six papers (the five Model Guess Papers plus the Bullet Model Paper, 199 slot-instances) WAS run on 2026-08-29: all 199 resolved to an authored card, and every one carried the section and marks its slot implies. That is a substitute corpus, not a board paper — it cannot show what the board asks that this book omits. The book shows the long division in a boxed layout; the card writes the same division as two subtraction lines and the product-plus-remainder identity x³ = (x − 1)(x² + x − 2) + 3x − 2, which a student can check by expanding. Truth check: expanding (x − 1)(x² + x − 2) + 3x − 2 = x³ − 3x + 2 + 3x − 2 = x³, and putting x = 0 in the remainder identity gives −2 = A(2) + B(−1) = 2/3 − 8/3 = −2 with A = 1/3, B = 8/3.

recall_prompt: Say how you would resolve x³/((x − 1)(x + 2)) into partial fractions — name each move in order, starting with what must be done before the form is written.
insider_note: Degree 3 over degree 2 is improper, so divide FIRST — quotient x − 1, remainder 3x − 2 — because no A and B can resolve x³ directly; the quotient must also appear again in the final line.

steps.label: Divide, then set up the form
steps.margin_note: First mark. The numerator has degree 3 and the denominator degree 2, so the fraction is IMPROPER. Divide first: quotient x − 1, remainder 3x − 2. Only the remainder fraction is resolved.
steps.memory_tip: Degree 3 over degree 2 — divide FIRST. Quotient x − 1, remainder 3x − 2; only the remainder is resolved.

recall.must_convey: That the fraction is improper, so x³ is divided by x² + x − 2 to give quotient x − 1 and remainder 3x − 2, and only (3x − 2)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) is written as A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 2).

steps.why: Partial fractions are defined only for proper fractions, where the numerator has lower degree. Dividing separates the polynomial part x − 1, and the remainder over the same denominator is proper and can be resolved.
common_mistakes: Writing x³/((x − 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 2) without dividing; no A and B can make that identity hold.
Getting the remainder as 3x + 2 or −3x − 2 by a sign error in the second subtraction.
Dividing by (x − 1)(x + 2) without expanding it to x² + x − 2 first.

steps.label: Clear the denominators
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Multiply the remainder fraction equation by (x − 1)(x + 2). The quotient x − 1 stays aside; it is not part of this identity.
steps.memory_tip: The left side of the identity is the REMAINDER 3x − 2, not x³. The quotient stays aside.

recall.must_convey: That multiplying the remainder equation through gives 3x − 2 = A(x + 2) + B(x − 1).
accept: multiply both sides by x minus one into x plus two to get three x minus two equals A into x plus two plus B into x minus one

steps.why: The identity is written for the proper fraction, whose numerator is the remainder 3x − 2, not x³. Using x³ here is the most common error in this question.
common_mistakes: Writing x³ = A(x + 2) + B(x − 1); the left side must be the remainder.
Carrying the quotient x − 1 into the identity.

steps.label: Find the constants
steps.margin_note: Third mark. x = 1 gives A = 1/3, x = −2 gives B = 8/3. Fractions with 3; keep them as fractions.
steps.memory_tip: Substitute into 3x − 2, not into x³: x = 1 gives A = 1/3 and x = −2 gives B = 8/3.

recall.must_convey: That x = 1 gives A = 1/3 and x = −2 gives B = 8/3.

steps.why: Each root of a linear factor makes the other term vanish and leaves one constant. Two factors, two roots, two constants, no simultaneous equations.
common_mistakes: Putting x = −2 and writing 3(−2) − 2 as −4 instead of −8.
Writing B = −8/3 by dropping the minus on (−2 − 1) = −3.
Putting x = 1 into x³ instead of into 3x − 2.

steps.label: Write the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The quotient x − 1 comes back in front of the two fractions. The answer has a polynomial part AND two fractions. Write the original fraction on the left.
steps.memory_tip: The quotient x − 1 returns in front. Check x = 0: −2 = 2/3 − 8/3.

recall.must_convey: That the fraction equals x − 1 + 1/(3(x − 1)) + 8/(3(x + 2)), with the quotient x − 1 in front.

steps.why: The quotient found in step 1 is part of the answer. Leaving it out gives the resolution of the remainder fraction, not of x³/((x − 1)(x + 2)).
common_mistakes: Forgetting the x − 1 in the final line.
Writing 1/3(x − 1) so it reads as one third times (x − 1); put the 3 in the denominator bracket.
Not checking: expand (x − 1)(x² + x − 2) + 3x − 2 and confirm it is x³; then put x = 0 in the identity, −2 = 2/3 − 8/3.
